COMMENTS: All known traces of textiles at Batujaya come from three graves belonging to the same group of twenty-three burials brought to light in sector A of the Segaran II mound (locally known as Unur Lempeng), during excavations carried out in 2005 (grave 4/Stratigraphic unit 109) and 2006 (grave 13/SU 186 and 18/SU 304). All three burials were excavated between 1.20 m and 1.65 m under the surface and are associated with early to mid-Buni phases of occupation of Batujaya, that is between the first century BCE and the second century CE. No collagen at all remained in bones or teeth, preventing a direct dating of the skeletons (probably due to the waterlogged environment, the burial layers having remained under the water table for centuries). Their age, however, can be deduced from the stratigraphic sequence and a series of radiocarbon dates obtained from organic material samples collected in corresponding stratigraphic units. Most bodies were buried in an extended position, lying on their backs (but disturbances brought about by successive burials often render their analysis difficult). None of the burials show traces of planks or biers having been used. Grave goods associated with skeletons comprised Buni ceramic ware, dishes of what appear to be, based on microscopy, coarse-fabric imitations of rouletted ware, gold, ivory and horn jewellery, iron tools, net sinkers and fish bones.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Anggreani, 1999, The introduction of metallurgy into Indonesia: a comparative study with special reference to Gilimanuk, Unpublished M.A. dissertation, Australian National University, Canberra. Bali
COMMENTS: This site has been claimed as a ceremonial site because of the presence of a large natural boulder at the top of the hill, surrounded by a number of artefacts that upon excavation were seemingly oriented in lines towards it, i.e. east-west. Some of those artefacts, found in square LP VIII, are composed of intact vessels and sherds, an iron spear-head, a gold foil mask above three Soejono II-B type bronze axes, an iron fragment and a bead. There is no information about the material of this bead, but until 1972, nineteen stone beads and forty-nine glass beads have been found, from 15 to 65 cm depth. In addition, a bronze bell, a bronze bowl, sticks of bronze with geometric ornamentation (and one with a human figure at the pointed end), gold ornaments and a number of earthenware pots, footed vessels and several ceremonial lamps were also found close to the large stone. The site was probably used in several successive periods, from late Neolithic, through protohistoric, historic and even into the period of Japanese colonisation (1942-1945), the latter represented by remains of fortifications. Pieces of obsidian and stone adzes have also been recovered from this site. The pottery from this site is fragile and rough, consisting of jars, small bowls on pedestals, and cooking pots. Decoration includes impression, circle stamping and incised lines. Bronze artefacts were found in thirteen squares, from 15 to 95 cm in depth. They comprise Soejono type II-A, II-B and VII axes, a pendant, a rod, and probably a buckle. Iron objects, scattered in twenty-two squares from 15 to 85 cm depth, consist of daggers and knives, rods, spearheads, wire and other unidentified fragments. Iron slag appeared in six squares, from 15 to 95 cm depth. In addition to these objects, two bronze axes, one anthropomorphic bronze figurine, one bronze rod, a fragment of a (possibly Heger I type) bronze drum, two bronze pendants, two iron hoes, one fragment of an iron tool and three iron spearheads, were found by a villager approximately 40 to 50 cm under the surface. Interestingly, remains of woven Pandanus fiber wrapping were still retained on one iron hoe and one bronze axe, and remains of similar wrapping overlain by textile were found on both surfaces of an iron spearhead with a bronze ring at its end. Another iron spearhead examined retained remains of a wooden scabbard on its surface. Chemical compositions of two bronze axes from Pasir Angin have been reported. More recent analyses have been done on the 1992 finds. These include a sheet bronze fragment, part of an axe blade, part of an axe shaft, and a rod-shaped bronze fragment. Pieces of obsidian were found in almost all of the squares, from 15 to 95 cm depth, including cores, debitage, and pieces with use-wear. The other stone tools are stone adzes and an adze blank, found in seven squares from 15 to 65 cm depth. While the majority of adzes are of silicified limestone, one is a well-polished chalcedony rectangular-sectioned adze, 18 cm long, found approximately 95 cm from the surface in square LP III. Remains of bovids were reported, but only in small amounts. Although not clearly stated, there is an indication that a small amount of human bone was also present in this site. Some questions emerge from the finding of iron slag and obsidian in Pasir Angin in subsurface levels. Were these associated, and how far was the site disturbed? Although Pasir Angin is normally claimed to be site of ceremonial depositions, it is more likely that it is a burial and habitation site from which all or most human bones has disappeared because the soil is acid.

COMMENTS: Description: The cultural heritage remains at this site consist of nine menhirs arranged in a pattern based on their size. The largest menhir is approximately 150 cm tall, the others are smaller and stacked with stones in formations resembling tombs, with the smaller menhirs serving as headstones. There are four tomb formations, each with two small menhirs, commonly called Pahoman. According to local folklore, the site is associated with King Pucuk Umun and his followers, who are said to have retreated and meditated at Pasir Peuteuy before continuing their journey to Cibeo. Some hold that Pucuk Umun and his followers are the ancestors of the present-day Baduy people, though this remains uncertain.

COMMENTS: Description: The Batu Goong site is named after several stone artefacts in the complex that resemble gamelan/kenong instruments (goong in Sundanese). The site is located in a hilly area called Kaduguling and is more commonly known locally as Batu Goong. The complex contains twelve stones grouped within a 5.3 x 5.3 m enclosure: one central menhir, ten flat-topped cylindrical stones (palinggih) arranged around it, and one small gong-shaped artefact (kenong). This formation is known as the temu gelang formation, commonly found in megalithic traditions. One additional stone artefact lies outside the enclosure but remains partially buried. The stones are protected by a BRC fence measuring 11.12 x 11.12 m and 1.2 m high. The cylindrical stones have a relatively consistent diameter of 50-52 cm, with varying heights.

COMMENTS: Description: The site features a block of andesite stone with a flat top resembling a bed, known as a dolmen. In megalithic tradition, dolmens serve as burial grounds or places of worship, the exact function at Batu Ranjang is unknown as no associated megalithic elements such as menhirs have been found. The dolmen is supported by four neatly crafted stones bearing circular pleated carvings, with a foundation beneath to prevent sinking. Its orientation is east-west, it measures approximately 258 cm long and 99 cm wide, and is made of andesite. Atop the dolmen are two stones: one round and one slightly oval (approximately 33 cm long and 20 cm wide). Two mortar stones, thought to have served as instruments of ancestral spirit worship, are located on the south and north sides of the dolmen respectively. The dolmen is similar in form to dolmens in the Sumba region used as graves.

COMMENTS: Description: The Cidaresi Scratched Stone is an andesite monolith measuring approximately 175 cm long and 102 cm wide, located in the middle of local rice fields. It bears triangular incised marks of varying sizes, each with a hole at the centre, collectively depicting a symbol interpreted by the local community as representing female genitals (kemaluan wanita), and understood as a symbol of fertility or purity. Fertility symbols were central to the rituals of farming and livestock-raising communities who believed their harvests and herds depended on the propitiation of ancestral spirits.

COMMENTS: Description: Sanghyang Heuleut consists of large upright menhirs of dense porous andesite measuring 150 cm high. Medium-sized andesite stones scattered among them form the menhir bases, arranged horizontally in a square formation (approximately 3 x 3 m) with a smaller menhir at each corner. Flat-surfaced stones were also found among the scattered stones. The site served as a place of worship for a megalithic culture community. Located near a river and in the middle of a plantation, the site has been fenced to prevent damage by animals and humans. Approximately 10 metres away is a second artefact known as the Sorban Stone, carved in the shape of a turban: 40 cm high, 30 cm radius, carved 5 cm thick. Smaller stones (2 x 2 m wide) and two upright stones approximately 50 cm high are scattered around it.

COMMENTS: Description: The obsidian discovery location at Bukit Unggul is located in a cinchona plantation landscape with workers' houses/emplacements clustered around it. At Poponcol, the stopping point/post towards Mount Koromong, the landscape consists of forest trees and bushes. The obsidian discovery location at Mount Koromong is located in a landscape of forest, gardens, and bushes with andesite boulders at the peak. Access to this location has been opened as a hiking and trail bike trail. Obsidian traces were found on the alternative/eastern trail (from the post/warung/downhill trail towards Situ Patahunan in the north) or approximately 200 m down from the peak. The location around the Legok Nangka TPPAS is an obsidian source location located close to the Kendan region. Obsidian traces in these two areas are very abundant and the most among the findings at other locations. The landscape consists of open land surrounded by plantations.
